text: Layer 1C ranking suggests the clearest Energy and Power Chain chokepoint cluster is electrical hardware plus execution: switchgear, substations, busway, electrical balance-of-system, qualified contractors, testing and commissioning.
Powell, Eaton, Hubbell and PLPC form a useful grid/electrical-hardware validation set, with Eaton/Hubbell as references and Powell/PLPC as more Serenity-style underfollowed or niche exposures.
MYR Group and IES Holdings should be tracked as execution-layer candidates because qualified electrical labor, procurement, substation construction and commissioning may be independent bottlenecks.

Nuclear should remain decomposed into fuel cycle, HALEU, uranium, qualified components, licensing and EPC; SMR developers should be treated as speculative shadow candidates until project evidence improves.
Layer 2 should verify market caps, revenue exposure, backlog, valuation, analyst coverage and source filings for all underfollowed candidates before narrowing the universe.
The current universe is still US-heavy and should be expanded with Canada, Europe, Japan, Korea and Taiwan suppliers in transformers, grid components, nuclear services, cooling and power electronics.

Several candidates were kept as hypotheses despite incomplete evidence because the Serenity method allows weak-evidence names into Layer 1 when they have explicit hidden signals and falsification paths.

Energy and Power Chain should be tracked as an end-to-end system: large-load demand -> load forecasting/resource adequacy -> interconnection/transmission -> substations -> transformers/switchgear -> electrical labor/commissioning -> dispatchable and clean firm generation -> power-market cost allocation.

Highest current bottleneck candidates are distribution/large power transformers, medium-voltage switchgear, interconnection/transmission, qualified electrical construction labor, and dispatchable generation slots.

Nuclear fuel-cycle exposure, especially HALEU enrichment and qualification, is a separate policy-driven bottleneck tied to advanced reactors and SMR optionality rather than near-term data-center energization.
Electrical equipment earnings with explicit data-center order growth, backlog growth, book-to-bill, capacity expansion, and margin durability should be monitored as primary catalysts.

FERC/RTO proceedings on large-load interconnection, capacity auctions, and cost allocation are likely to determine how much data-center power demand is monetized by utilities, IPPs, generators, and equipment suppliers.

Need source-backed mapping of low-attention public companies to specific grid hardware SKUs, substation components, distributor channels, testing/certification gates, and utility-approved-vendor status.
Need to distinguish true bottleneck revenue from general construction cyclicality for specialty electrical contractors and balance-of-system suppliers.
Need regional mapping of data-center load growth by RTO/ISO, transformer/switchgear lead times, generation retirements, and transmission constraints to avoid overgeneralizing national demand.

Do not let Eaton, GE Vernova, Vertiv, Constellation, and other high-attention leaders dominate the map; use them as demand validators while continuing to search for underfollowed suppliers one or two nodes upstream or downstream.

Project delays, canceled data-center builds, or procurement prepayments caused by unavailable power equipment should be treated as positive evidence for bottleneck severity but negative evidence for immediate load realization.

POWL maps directly to the medium-voltage switchgear, integrated power-control-room, e-house, substation, bus duct, and data-center electrical distribution bottleneck; verify backlog conversion, customer concentration, and execution margin before upgrading.
ETN should remain the reference validation ticker for Electrical Americas backlog, data-center electrical order growth, and electrification demand; do not treat it as underfollowed.

GEV should remain the reference validation ticker for gas-turbine scarcity plus grid equipment demand; use its backlog and lead-time commentary to validate or falsify dispatchable-generation bottlenecks.
LEU maps to the nuclear fuel-cycle/HALEU bottleneck, but evidence must focus on DOE support, licensing, commercial demand, capacity milestones, and funding rather than generic nuclear enthusiasm.
PLPC is a second-order underfollowed grid hardware candidate; the key question is whether substation/HV/EHV and Delta Star-related exposure are material enough to matter.

MYRG and IESC belong in the electrical labor/execution bottleneck lane, but both need backlog and project-mix verification to avoid confusing broad construction cyclicality with AI/grid power infrastructure exposure.

VRT, CEG, and HUBB are reference or semi-reference names used to price the market's view of data-center infrastructure, clean firm power, and utility grid hardware; they should not crowd out smaller supplier discovery.

Need primary-source SEC filings, earnings presentations, transcripts, and investor decks for POWL, PLPC, MYRG, IESC, HUBB, VRT, GEV, LEU, and CEG before Layer 3 scoring; current mapping relies partly on cached Layer 1 evidence.
Need live market-cap, valuation, analyst-coverage, short-interest, and earnings-revision checks to separate true underfollowed candidates from already-consensus winners.

Need falsification tracking for lead-time normalization, backlog cancellations, customer capex digestion, fixed-price contract margin compression, capacity additions, commodity pressure, and regulatory delay.

PWR should remain a reference benchmark for grid execution and qualified electrical labor, not an underfollowed alpha candidate, until backlog, labor and margin evidence show a stronger chokepoint premium.

BWXT is a priority underfollowed nuclear-supply-chain hypothesis because generalists may classify it as defense/government nuclear exposure, but its commercial nuclear/SMR/materiality evidence must be verified before promotion.
CCJ is best used as a nuclear fuel-cycle reference leader and pricing benchmark rather than an underfollowed discovery name.
SMR should remain in the speculative_shadow lane because project financing, customer commitments, licensing, cost and construction timelines are the decisive survival tests.

VST, NRG, ETR, SO, NEE and BEPC are mostly power-asset or regulated/contracted generation mappings; they validate demand and power-market tightness but are less direct physical bottleneck suppliers than transformers, switchgear, construction labor or nuclear fuel/components.
FLNC remains an underfollowed storage/flexibility hypothesis, but margin quality, warranty risk, battery sourcing and backlog conversion are gating evidence items.

Need primary-source SEC filings and latest earnings materials for every ticker in this chunk; current company-specific evidence is sparse except for broader grid-demand context and Eaton electrical backlog references from cached Layer 2A evidence.
Need current market-cap, valuation, analyst coverage and price-performance checks to distinguish true underfollowed names from already-consensus AI power beneficiaries.
Need regional evidence for power-asset names: PJM/ERCOT/Southeast/Gulf Coast load growth, capacity-market outcomes, hedging, rate cases, IRPs and large-load contracts.
Need nuclear-specific evidence for BWXT, CCJ and SMR: DOE awards, NRC licensing, HALEU/fuel-cycle constraints, signed customer contracts, component qualification and project financing.

FIX should be promoted within this candidate chunk as the clearest visible execution-bottleneck mapping: data-center/technology-sector mechanical and electrical contracting demand, FY2025 technology-sector strength, electrical-segment growth, and backlog growth are directly disclosed.

ENS remains an underfollowed critical-power candidate: industrial battery label may obscure mission-critical backup exposure, but data-center/telecom/utility segment materiality must be proven before ranking it above core grid hardware names.

AZZ is a second-order grid-buildout candidate through galvanizing/metal coatings for critical infrastructure; the key survival test is whether utility/transmission/electrical infrastructure is a material volume and pricing driver.

GNRC has plausible backup-power and distributed-resilience exposure, including telecom and potential data-center demand, but residential generator cyclicality and outage-driven demand make it less pure than grid hardware or data-center electrical contractors.

ENPH and SEDG are real distributed-energy power-electronics companies, but their relationship to the Energy and Power Chain is grid-edge flexibility rather than AI data-center critical-path power infrastructure; both require market-pricing and residential-solar-cycle checks.

TTEK, ACM, J, and APG are services/execution reference or underfollowed candidates. They may benefit from permitting, engineering, water, fire/safety, and infrastructure maintenance bottlenecks, but each needs end-market/backlog materiality verification.

STEM, SEDG, and CBAT should remain speculative_shadow until financial-quality gates are passed. STEM has going-concern and working-capital concerns; CBAT has low gross margin and customer/product-validation risk; SEDG needs proof of durable recovery from prior solar-channel stress.
Need current market-cap, valuation, analyst-coverage, short-interest, and earnings-revision checks for every ticker before classifying them as truly underfollowed or already consensus.
Need latest 2026 quarterly reports and transcripts for FIX, ENS, GNRC, AZZ, ENPH, SEDG, STEM, CBAT, TTEK, ACM, J, and APG to confirm whether FY2025 evidence continued into 2026.
Candidate chunk visible to the model was truncated after APi Group; later Layer 2B calls should verify whether additional tickers were omitted from this chunk before final scoring.

FLS is the strongest underfollowed candidate in this chunk for deeper Layer 2C work because its pumps, valves, seals, and flow-control exposure could touch power generation, nuclear, cooling, LNG, and aftermarket reliability, but company-specific materiality is still unverified.

GTLS remains a plausible underfollowed second-order gas/LNG/fuel-infrastructure candidate, but it should not be promoted until backlog and orders show linkage to power generation, backup fuel, grid reliability, or data-center load growth.

KMI and WMB should be treated as reference benchmarks for the gas-infrastructure lane, not primary underfollowed discoveries; their main function is to test whether power demand is flowing into contracted midstream projects.

AMSC, EOSE, NNE, and OKLO belong in the speculative shadow lane until primary evidence validates commercial scalability, customer validation, financing, regulatory milestones, and margin/unit economics.

WSC and WFRD are indirect second-order exposures and should be deprioritized unless filings or transcripts explicitly show power, grid, data-center, or gas-fired generation demand as a measurable driver.

Need primary-source verification for all company-level claims using latest 10-K, 10-Q, earnings transcripts, investor presentations, project announcements, customer disclosures, FERC/NRC/DOE records, and backlog/order data.
Need current market-cap, valuation, analyst-coverage, short-interest, and ownership checks before confirming which names are genuinely underfollowed versus already priced as AI power beneficiaries.

Need falsification triggers per ticker: lack of theme-specific revenue disclosure, no backlog conversion, customer cancellations, inability to finance capacity, licensing delays, gross-margin deterioration, or management commentary showing demand is unrelated to power-load growth.
